title: Train a model, then use it in Python

---
order: 1
unit: start
title: Train a model, then use it in Python
summary: Train a tiny picture model in the Pattern Trainer, download it as my_model.json, see it answer on the board, then load the same file in a Python starter and see a prediction there.
language: python
recipes: [import-module, dotted-call, none, attribute]
hook: "Phones sort your photos into people, pets and food without anyone writing a rule for what a dog looks like. Someone trained a model on examples, then put it inside an app. That second part is what you'll do in these projects."
---
In these projects your app uses a model **you** train. The training happens in the **Pattern Trainer**, a web page; the model then goes into a Python app on your computer as one file, `my_model.json`. This lesson does that once, with something small, so you know the whole path before you start a project.

## Predict

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students expect a model to say it doesn't know. Committing first makes the confident wrong answer on the board stick."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "You train a model on 10 photos of your pencil case and 10 of your water bottle. Then you show it a banana. What will it say?"
  options: ["Pencil case or water bottle, maybe very sure", "I don't know", "Banana", "Nothing: it waits for a photo it knows"]
  actual: "Pencil case or water bottle, and often very sure. A model always picks one of the classes it was trained on; it has no idea of 'something else' unless you give it a class for that."
```

## Train and try

```step
stage: run
insight: "Seeing a model they trained a minute ago answer on photos it has never seen makes 'a model learns from examples' concrete, and sets up the confident wrong answer."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#open", height: 760 }
check: { type: board, text: "Open your model file, add at least 4 photos it has never seen, and see what it says.", when: "n_classes >= 2 and n_photos >= 4" }
```

1. Open the [Pattern Trainer](https://tools.learningwaypoints.com/trainer/) in a new tab and choose **Pictures**. Name the first class after something on your desk, then **+ Add a class** for a second thing.
2. Hold each thing up to the camera and **Hold to record** about 10 photos per class, moving it a little. Click **Train model**.
3. Click **Download my_model.json**. On the board, click **Open your model file** and choose it.
4. Add a few photos the model **hasn't** seen: each thing somewhere else, and one thing that is neither. Which does it get right? How sure is it about the one that is neither?

The photos stay on your computer: the trainer and the board work inside the browser, and the model file holds only your class names and numbers.

## Investigate

```step
stage: investigate
code: classify.py#classify
insight: "The starter is short because pattern_model.py hides the hard part. What students change is a threshold and a message, which is where the app's judgement lives."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "What is in my_model.json?"
      options: ["Your class names and a lot of numbers", "Your photos, shrunk", "A link to your model online", "Python code"]
      answer: 0
      explain: "The trainer turned each photo into numbers, trained on those, and saved only the class names and the trained numbers. No photo can be rebuilt from them."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "model.top(image) gives back (\"Pencil case\", 0.62). What does the app say?"
      options: ["Might be Pencil case, but I'm not confident (0.62).", "Pencil case (0.62 confidence)", "Upload or take a photo first.", "It crashes: 0.62 is not a whole number"]
      answer: 0
      explain: "0.62 is less than 0.8, so the if branch runs and the app says it isn't sure."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Where do the class names in the app come from?"
      options: ["From my_model.json, so you never type them", "From the names of your photo files", "From the classify function", "You type them into the starter"]
      answer: 0
      explain: "PatternModel.load reads them from the file, in the same order as the trainer. Rename a class in the trainer, download again, and the app follows."
```

This is the part of the starter `image_pattern_trainer.py` that answers. `pattern_model.py` does the hard part, exactly as the trainer did: centre square, picture to numbers, then your trained numbers.

### Inside the model file

Open your `my_model.json` in a text editor (Notepad or TextEdit) and scroll through it.

### What the app says

`model.top(image)` gives back two things: the most likely class and how sure the model is, from 0 to 1. Follow them through the `if`.

### Where the class names come from

The starter never types Cat, Coffee or your own class names.

## Run it in Python

```step
stage: make
insight: "The same file giving the same answer in Python shows the model is just data an app can carry."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I ran image_pattern_trainer.py with my own my_model.json, gave it a photo, and got an answer from my model." }
```

1. [Set up the starters](https://github.com/edu-matthew-pham/pattern-detector-starters#set-up-once) on your computer, if your teacher hasn't already.
2. Put **your** `my_model.json` in the starters folder, replacing the sample (Cat vs Coffee).
3. Run `python image_pattern_trainer.py` and open the address it prints (usually `http://127.0.0.1:7860`).
4. Give it one of the photos you tried on the board. It should give the same class and nearly the same confidence.

Then change the `# ADAPT:` lines: a message that would help someone, and a threshold that suits your test photos. That is where Brief B starts.

```teacher
summary: Students train a two-class picture model in the Pattern Trainer, test
  it on the board on photos it hasn't seen, read the starter's classify
  function, and run the same my_model.json in the Python starter on their own
  computer.
time: 40
timing: Predict 3 min · Train and try 12 min · Investigate 10 min · Run it in
  Python 15 min
goals:
  - I can train a picture model and download it as my_model.json.
  - I can test a model on photos it has never seen and say how sure it is.
  - I can load my model in a Python app and change what it says.
before: |
  **The idea:** a model is trained on examples in one place (the Pattern Trainer, a web page) and used in another (a Python app), and what travels between them is one small file of class names and numbers. This lesson does that path once, with two things from the student's desk, before any project.

  **Before class:** the starters need installing once per computer (Python 3, then `pip install -r requirements.txt`, about 0.5 GB, no TensorFlow; [setup](https://github.com/edu-matthew-pham/pattern-detector-starters#set-up-once)). Do it before the lesson, or the last step becomes an install lesson. On a student laptop on the school network, check tools.learningwaypoints.com/trainer/ loads (about 35 MB the first time, for the trainer and again for the board) and the camera is allowed. Without a camera, students use **Upload photos** with photos they have.

  **Privacy:** training happens in the browser and photos never leave the computer (the trainer's Privacy page shows how to check). The board keeps students' test photos in this browser only. `my_model.json` holds class names and numbers, no photos. Train on things, not people.

  **Where this sits:** the first step of Pattern Detector projects, after Apps with Gradio. It needs Gradio apps, `if`/`else` and f-strings; the trainer does the training and `pattern_model.py` hides numpy. Machine learning with Gradio shows how a model works inside; either can come first.
running:
  - "Predict: take a show of hands. Most say 'I don't know'."
  - "Train and try: 10 minutes. Ask: what did it say about the thing that was
    neither, and how sure was it?"
  - "Investigate: everyone opens my_model.json in a text editor. Point out there
    is no photo in it."
  - "Run it in Python: pair students whose install worked with those whose
    didn't."
stuck:
  - see: The board says the file is not a model file, or is a project file.
    ask: Did you click Download my_model.json (not Save project)?
    fix: Download the model and open my_model.json.
  - see: The board or the trainer says the picture model didn't load.
    ask: Can this computer open tools.learningwaypoints.com?
    fix: Ask for the site to be allowed on the school network, then reload.
  - see: The Python app still says Cat or Coffee.
    ask: Which my_model.json is in the starters folder?
    fix: Replace the sample with your download (same name, my_model.json), then run
      the app again.
  - see: "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mediapipe' (or gradio)."
    ask: Is the starters' .venv switched on in this terminal?
    fix: Activate .venv (see the setup), or run pip install -r requirements.txt.
stretch: Add a third class, Neither, with photos of other things. Does the thing
  that was neither now get the right answer?
support: Train in pairs on one laptop; skip the Python step and do it at the
  start of Brief B.
leads: "Next: Brief B (a model you train) builds an app around this model; Brief
  A (rules you write) can come first. Real world: photo apps, recycling sorters
  and parcel scanners are a trained model inside an app."
exit:
  q: What is inside my_model.json, and why can the same file work in the trainer,
    on the board and in Python?
  a: Class names and the trained numbers. Each side turns a picture into numbers
    the same way, then runs the same trained numbers on them.
explain: >
  A **model** is trained on examples, then used inside an app.


  - The **Pattern Trainer** turns each photo into numbers and learns from them.

  - **my_model.json** keeps only your class names and the trained numbers: no
  photos.

  - In Python, `model.top(image)` gives the most likely class and how sure the
  model is (0 to 1).

  - A model always picks one of its classes, so the app's **threshold** decides
  when to say it isn't sure.
struggle: Moving the downloaded file into the starters folder in place of the
  sample. Ask students to say out loud which folder the app reads from before
  they run it.
```

# Open the model file the student just downloaded, and test it on a few photos it has not seen (kept in this browser).

# region: open
widget: classifier
testset: own
webcam: on
# endregion
files.classify.py:
# The part of the starters' image_pattern_trainer.py that answers (display only: it needs the starters to run).

# region: classify
from pattern_model import PatternModel

model = PatternModel.load("my_model.json")
print("Classes in this model:", model.classes)


def classify(image):
    if image is None:
        return "Upload or take a photo first."
    label, score = model.top(image)
    if score < 0.8:
        return f"Might be {label}, but I'm not confident ({score:.2f})."
    else:
        return f"{label} ({score:.2f} confidence)"
# endregion
